title: The World's Largest Electric Aircraft Just Flew: $5 of Electricity, Taking On Regional Aviation
dek: Heart Aerospace's ES-30 electric aircraft takes off on $5 of electricity, with operating costs 48% lower than the old planes it replaces, targeting half of the world's flights under two hours and using hybrid power to solve the backup battery problem.
why: This episode shows the seven-year journey from a 3D-printed model to a 100-foot wingspan aircraft, revealing the economics and technical breakthroughs of electric aviation — highly illuminating for listeners focused on clean energy and transportation innovation.
who: Founders, investors and engineers focused on clean energy, aviation technology and startup financing.

points.h: The electric aircraft's electricity bill is just $5
points.body: The world's largest electric aircraft, Heart Aerospace's ES-30, has completed its first flight. It has a 100-foot wingspan and a takeoff weight of 25,000 pounds, yet takeoff costs only $5 in electricity. Its all-electric range is 125 miles, 500 miles with hybrid power, and charging takes about 30 minutes. This marks the viability of electric aviation in the regional market, with operating costs 48% lower than conventional aircraft.

Heart's aircraft replaces jet engines with electric motors. A motor has only one moving part, no combustion, and almost zero wear, so it is cheaper to produce and more reliable. A jet engine, by contrast, has thousands of parts and burns fuel at extremely high temperatures. Electric motors are nearly silent while taxiing and have good torque characteristics, significantly reducing noise and vibration.

points.h: Regional aviation has been ignored by technology
points.body: The complexity of jet engines makes the engine cost for a 30-seat and a 70-seat aircraft similar, which pushes airlines toward larger aircraft and longer routes, leaving short regional flights extremely inefficient. Half of the world's flights are under two hours, but existing technology cannot serve this market effectively. Heart is targeting 40-year-old aircraft; the key to regional connectivity is flight cost, not distance.

points.h: From a Swedish air force base to MIT
points.body: Anders grew up next to a Swedish air force base, passionate about aircraft, and later pursued a PhD in jet engines at MIT. Twelve years ago, Elon Musk spoke at MIT and said all forms of transportation would become electric — this became his inspiration. He began researching jet engines by day and tinkering with drones at night, and with Swedish government funding built a relationship with Nordic airlines, laying the foundation for his startup.

points.h: YC startup: from LOI to physical hardware
points.body: At YC, Anders started with a 3D-printed model and letters of intent (LOIs) from airlines including SAS. They first built a 400-kilowatt motor, which attracted a pre-order from United Airlines and in turn more capital. Anders stresses that every fundraise needs substantive progress, ideally something physical you can touch — that is more persuasive than a business plan.

points.h: United came from the spam folder
points.body: Heart's first big customer, United Airlines, came out of the spam folder. Clara, while clearing spam, found the inbound email and invited them to visit. After they demonstrated the electric motor, United understood immediately and placed an order. This shows the importance of showing the physical object directly, and that unconventional channels can bring huge opportunities.

At its Los Angeles factory, Heart designs and builds most of the aircraft's components itself, including actuators and the fuselage. They chose to make key parts in-house to avoid depending on a single supplier and to accelerate iteration. The whole factory is like one big test bench, where faults can be injected to verify that systems still run safely under abnormal conditions.

Heart's battery lab tests cells from manufacturers in China, the US and South Korea; the current highest energy density is 370 Wh/kg, close to the 400 Wh/kg target. To solve the backup battery problem, they use a hybrid system with a simple turboprop engine as backup, adding about 20% to upfront cost but letting the aircraft fly 500 miles and meet safety reserve requirements.

Heart borrows SpaceX's risk-management philosophy: focus on minimizing the impact of errors rather than avoiding risk entirely. They are not building air taxis but attacking the mainstream aircraft market directly, with 36 seats and the existing infrastructure of 5,000 airports. Compared with hydrogen, hybrid electric already has a significant green premium advantage, and the aircraft appreciates over time like a house.
